cases.label: 10 A load
cases.reference: For the stated resistivity, each 20 m conductor has resistance 0.1376 Ω. The outgoing and return conductors form a 0.2752 Ω loop; at 10 A the loop drops 2.752 V. The 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m² area equals 2.5 mm². Connection and temperature effects are excluded.

cases.label: No-load check
cases.reference: The same conductor loop carries zero current, so neither conductor has a resistive voltage drop. This does not include external induced voltage or connection effects.

cases.label: Increasing positive flux
cases.reference: Flux linkage increases by 200 × 0.003 = 0.6 Wb-turn in 0.1 s. Faraday’s law gives an average emf of −6 V in the chosen winding reference; reversing the flux change reverses this signed emf.

cases.label: Decreasing flux
cases.reference: The winding loses 0.6 Wb-turn of flux linkage in 0.1 s. The induced average emf is +6 V in the same winding reference.

cases.label: Unchanged flux
cases.reference: No change in flux linkage over the nonzero interval means zero induced average emf. A nonzero static magnetic field alone does not create a Faraday emf in this stationary winding.

cases.label: Rising current
cases.reference: A 0.2 H inductance gains 0.6 Wb-turn of linkage as current rises by 3 A. Over 0.05 s the signed back emf is −12 V. With the passive terminal-voltage convention the corresponding voltage is +12 V; these signs describe different references.

cases.label: Falling current
cases.reference: Current falls by 3 A in 0.05 s, so the inductor loses 0.6 Wb-turn of linkage. The signed back emf is +12 V in this expression’s reference, opposing the decrease.

cases.label: Constant current
cases.reference: With constant L and no current change, linkage is unchanged and the ideal inductive back emf is zero. Winding resistance is outside this model.

cases.label: Moving active segments
cases.reference: Each perpendicular 0.5 m segment moving at 3 m/s sweeps 1.5 m² of area per second. In a 0.4 T field that is 0.6 Wb/s, or 0.6 V per segment. Ten additive active segments give a 6 V magnitude.

cases.label: Stationary segments
cases.reference: Zero segment speed means zero swept area per second, so this motional-emf contribution is zero. Time-varying magnetic fields are a separate induction mechanism.

cases.label: Passive RL time constant
cases.reference: For a 0.5 H inductor with a closed 5 Ω discharge path, Kirchhoff’s balance gives di/dt = −10i per second. Current therefore falls by a factor of e in 0.1 s. This finite positive time constant assumes L>0 and R>0.

cases.label: Positive current
cases.reference: During a slow ideal current ramp from 0 to 3 A, flux linkage rises linearly from 0 to 1.2 Wb-turn. Integrating linkage against current gives the triangular area 1.2 × 3 / 2 = 1.8 J stored in the magnetic field.

cases.label: Reversed current
cases.reference: Reversing a linear inductor’s current reverses its magnetic field, but stored field energy remains positive. The equal-magnitude ramp to −3 A stores the same 1.8 J as the +3 A case.

cases.label: Zero current
cases.reference: Zero current in this linear ideal inductor gives zero magnetic field and zero stored magnetic energy.

cases.label: Pure sine reference
cases.reference: For a zero-offset sine with peak 10√2 A, the mean square over one cycle is 100 A². Its root is 10 A RMS. The separate reference test integrates the squared waveform numerically; this peak/RMS relation does not apply to arbitrary waveforms.

cases.label: Balanced star phasors
cases.reference: Take two 230 V RMS phase phasors separated by 120°. Their rectangular difference is (345, 199.18584) V, whose length is approximately 398.37169 V. This is a phasor difference, not 230 + 230 V.

cases.label: Balanced delta phasors
cases.reference: At one delta junction, subtract two equal 12 A branch-current phasors separated by 120°. The rectangular difference has components 18 A and 10.392305 A, giving approximately 20.78461 A line-current magnitude.

cases.label: Zero branch currents
cases.reference: With both relevant branch-current phasors zero, their difference and the line current are zero.

cases.label: Three identical phase loads
cases.reference: For a balanced star load, each branch has 230 V RMS and 10 A RMS, giving 2300 VA per phase. Three identical phases total 6900 VA. The matching line voltage is approximately 398.37169 V; line current is 10 A. This is apparent power, not active watts.

cases.label: Step-down winding ratio
cases.reference: Five groups of 100 primary turns correspond to one 100-turn secondary winding, so the primary/secondary turns ratio is 5. Under ideal equal volts-per-turn conditions, 500 V at the primary corresponds to 100 V at the secondary.

cases.label: Step-up winding ratio
cases.reference: The primary has one fifth as many turns as the secondary. The primary/secondary ratio is 0.2, and the ideal secondary winding voltage is five times the primary winding voltage.

cases.label: Ideal current and power balance
cases.reference: An ideal transformer with 500 V and 2 A at its primary transfers 1000 VA. At a 100 V secondary, equal apparent power requires 10 A. The secondary/primary current ratio is 10/2 = 5, consistent with a primary/secondary turns ratio of 5. Excitation and losses are excluded.
